passed.title: pl.row_index restarts at 0 inside each group
passed.trap: `pl.row_index` numbers rows within the current evaluation context. Inside `DataFrame.group_by(...).agg(...)` it restarts at 0 for each group, so it does not give the original row positions. If you need the original positions, call `DataFrame.with_row_index` before grouping and aggregate that column. The dtype is the index type (`u32` by default), not `i64`. The function is also marked unstable.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "B"]})

# Trap: positions are per group, not the original row numbers
print(df.group_by("x", maintain_order=True).agg(pl.row_index()))

# Right: materialise the original row index before grouping
print(
    df.with_row_index("idx")
    .group_by("x", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(pl.col("idx"))
)

print(df.select(pl.row_index()).schema)

passed.title: pl.time_range includes both endpoints and defaults end to the end of the day
passed.trap: `pl.time_range` and `pl.time_ranges` default to `closed='both'`, so the `end` value is included. This differs from Python's `range` and pandas-style half-open slicing. Pass `closed='left'` for a half-open range. If you omit `end`, it defaults to `time(23,59,59,999999)`, so the range silently runs to midnight.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import time

both = pl.time_range(time(9), time(12), "1h", eager=True)
left = pl.time_range(time(9), time(12), "1h", closed="left", eager=True)
no_end = pl.time_range(time(22), interval="1h", eager=True)

print(both.to_list())    # includes 12:00
print(left.to_list())    # stops at 11:00
print(no_end.to_list())  # runs to the end of the day

[datetime.time(9, 0), datetime.time(10, 0), datetime.time(11, 0)]
[datetime.time(22, 0), datetime.time(23, 0)]

passed.title: pl.union does not preserve row order; use pl.concat when order matters
passed.trap: `pl.union` looks like `pl.concat` and takes the same `how` strategies. However, it explicitly does not guarantee any ordering of rows in the result. Code that assumes the rows of the first frame come first, or relies on positional alignment afterwards, can silently get wrong results. Use `pl.concat` when you need predictable order, or sort the union result explicitly.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pl.DataFrame({"id": [3, 4]})

u = pl.union([a, b])
# Only rely on the union's content, not its order: sort explicitly
print(u.sort("id")["id"].to_list())

# pl.concat guarantees a's rows followed by b's rows
print(pl.concat([a, b])["id"].to_list())

passed.title: pl.scan_parquet raises on missing columns by default; allow_missing_columns is deprecated
passed.trap: When scanning several parquet sources whose schemas differ, `pl.scan_parquet` uses `missing_columns='raise'` by default. A later file that lacks a column from the first file therefore errors. The old `allow_missing_columns=True` flag is deprecated since 1.30.0. Pass `missing_columns='insert'` instead to fill the absent columns with nulls.

note.title: pl.threadpool_size is deprecated; call pl.thread_pool_size
note.trap: `pl.threadpool_size` was renamed in 0.20.7 and now emits a deprecation warning. Use `pl.thread_pool_size` instead. The pool size cannot be changed from Python after import. Only the `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` environment variable, set before process start, overrides it.
note.example:
import warnings
import polars as pl

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    old = pl.threadpool_size()
    print(w[0].category.__name__)

new = pl.thread_pool_size()
print(old == new, type(new).__name__)
